Apple today described a new UK proposal targeting App Store fees as price control, warning it could harm innovation and investment. Details below.

Apple opposes App Store regulation in the UK

According to Reuters, Apple today formally responded to a consultation by the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment methods.

The CMA may issue the rules after last year designating Apple and Google as having "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, such designations allow regulators to introduce company-specific rules to promote competition and give consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still take a commission on transactions completed through alternative payment methods, but any related fees must be considered "fair and reasonable".

Reuters noted that the CMA "expects the cost of steering fees to be lower than current App Store fees, and that the savings would be passed on to UK consumers or reinvested in developer businesses to support innovation".

Apple, however, disagrees and is opposing the proposal. Here's what Reuters reported:

The CMA rejected Apple's characterisation of the proposal as price control, saying its aim was to establish principles for determining whether steering fees are fair and reasonable, rather than directly setting fee levels.
